what_its_for: Pseudoephedrine is a decongestant that helps relieve a stuffy or blocked nose caused by colds, allergies, hay fever, or sinus congestion. It works by shrinking the blood vessels in your nasal passages so you can breathe more easily.
how_to_take: Take pseudoephedrine by mouth with a full glass of water. You may take it with or without food, but if it upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or milk. Swallow extended-release (long-acting) tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. If you have a regular immediate-release tablet, you may take it every 4 to 6 hours as directed. Keep in mind that this medicine is kept behind the pharmacy counter and requires you to show ID to purchase it.
dosing: Adults and children 12 years and older: The usual dose for immediate-release tablets is 60 mg every 4 to 6 hours. Do not take more than 240 mg in 24 hours. For 12-hour extended-release tablets, the dose is 120 mg every 12 hours. For 24-hour extended-release tablets, the dose is 240 mg once daily. Children under 12 years: Ask your doctor or pharmacist before giving this medicine to a child, as dosing depends on the child's weight and age.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and you remember within an hour or so, take it as soon as you can. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Since this medicine is usually taken as needed for symptoms, a strict schedule may not apply — take it only when you have nasal congestion.
storage: Store pseudoephedrine at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking pseudoephedrine within 14 days of using a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, or selegiline — this combination can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure. Avoid caffeine, energy drinks, and other stimulants while taking this medicine, as they can increase side effects like jitteriness, rapid heartbeat, and difficulty sleeping. Do not take other cold, allergy, or decongestant products at the same time without checking with your pharmacist, since many contain pseudoephedrine already. Avoid taking it close to bedtime, as it may make it hard to fall asleep.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: chest pain or a pounding, fast, or irregular heartbeat; severe headache or dizziness; shortness of breath; difficulty urinating or no urine output; severe nervousness or anxiety; numbness or weakness on one side of your body; or vision changes. Also call your doctor if your stuffy nose does not improve after 7 days, gets worse, or comes with a fever, rash, or persistent headache — these may be signs of a more serious condition.
when_it_works: Pseudoephedrine usually starts to relieve nasal congestion within 30 minutes of taking an immediate-release tablet. Extended-release versions may take a bit longer to start working but last longer throughout the day. You should feel noticeably less congested within the first hour of taking it.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Use with caution, as older adults are more sensitive to side effects like dizziness, high blood pressure, difficulty urinating, and fast heartbeat. Use the lowest effective dose and talk to your doctor first. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before using pseudoephedrine if you are pregnant, especially during the first trimester, as it may affect blood flow. Breastfeeding: Pseudoephedrine passes into breast milk and may reduce milk supply. Talk to your doctor before using if you are breastfeeding. People with certain health conditions: Do not use pseudoephedrine without talking to your doctor first if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, diabetes, thyroid disease (hyperthyroidism), an enlarged prostate, glaucoma, or kidney disease.
